blocks.x: We're recording today at 418 North Prairie Street. Today is February of the what? February.
I'll make you get a bit of a description of this drama you got here, Alfred. Duplex me, couldn't I?
I was a real boy. You say you played every, what, what's the room?

Every Christmas night we played at the St. Charles Hotel for years. Who was that called? I never know the name of the club, it was some big rich club. But we would start playing from around November the 1st. We would play the introduction nearly to all the debutants at different places, you know. And we'd be playing every night spot job different places from about November the 1st until Mardi Gras night. Mardi Gras day, we'd play at the Boston club, the same job that Celestine had. Mardi Gras day and Mardi Gras night. The Monday before Mardi Gras we played at Boston club. And we had the country club at one time for every Saturday night, 52 Saturday nights. That's right. Then in about January we'd have the T's. They'd have T's from January, the first something till around about the latter part of February. That was two hours from five to seven a T. And we had a large band, ten pieces. Yeah. Right. Right. Right. I just always say now, them fellas should be living today. Look at the money they could be making today, just living today. Yes, indeed. What about that job with Pete?
You say you got Mardi Gras day? Mardi Gras day?

That's at the Mont Leon Hotel. Now I don't know what room, but it's in one of the large rooms. He even had this same job playing for these people about sixteen years. They used to play at the patio royal. But after the crowd got so big, well he had to move over to the Mont Leon Hotel in one of the ballrooms. Which one? I don't know. There's three of them. You don't have any more questions?
Yeah, well I'll finish my broad at the end.
You get through yours first.
Oh God, well I got so many, I haven't seen it. But I'll, alright, well let's swap places then. I was wondering about guys like Sam Morgan and Blank Fatigue.
Did they ever play parades?

Yeah, uh-huh. They played parades. They played parades with different brass bands, you know. They'd hire them, you know, like a trumpet player wouldn't, couldn't make it. They'd hire them, you know, see. But they'd hire them to play fumes. They would play parades, you know, but you ain't playing nothing, you know. But funerals, they wouldn't hire them, you know. Sam couldn't read well enough to play a funeral, in other words. Buddy either. He could play if you're playing the hymns, you know, like we played, you know. Uh-huh. Things like that. But when it comes to them dodges, no, they couldn't make it.
Well, did they have any other brass bands? Oh, yeah. Who were some of the other ones?
Allen. Old Man Allen. Tulane, Amos Riley. Mm-hmm.
Did they have any strictly head brass bands?

Well, just jazz like, you know. Yeah. Most of them bands tried to read them dodges. Yeah. Most of them bands, old Man Allen. All them that couldn't, he'd always get the men that could read, you see. Yeah. That's one thing.
They always wanted to play them dodges. Oh, yeah.

Yeah. And now some guys like Foster, you know, they would get a brass band. Maybe he might know some people uptown got a club or borrow them or something, they're picking up some money, you know, to get a band, you know, like the Caledonia do, you know, see. Well they would pick up anybody and go ahead and play the funeral, you know, play them funeral marches by head, you know, lead me savior, narrow my God to thee, you know, and that was it. That was all. You see they could play. But when it comes down to real, dodges, I don't know. What would they play coming back in those bands? Well they played Denny Rambo, you know, see, and that was before Saints, you know, see, and other different things. But Sing On, that was the first hymn I heard them play Sing On. That was the first hymn, well after the little bands got that, but we never did play them for dances. No, we played for dances. Saints was the only first hymn that I heard the bands play. Yeah.
Kind of skipping around a little bit. Did you ever work at Pete Lawrence? Yeah, I worked at Pete Lawrence.

When he was at Murray and Iterville. Yeah, I worked there. When I worked there in 19, about 17, 16, I believe in part of 17. How I come to work there, Joe Oliver had the job. Well Joe Oliver went with Ory's band at that time. See, now like Saturday nights and Sunday nights he played with Ory. Well he put me down there, Steve Lewis, Lewis Armstrong, Morris French, you heard of Morris French. Old man Valto, you heard of him, was playing violin. And who was on piano? Well Steve, I told you Steve was on piano. Must have been about four or five pieces.
Well who was in Joe Oliver's band when he was at Pete Lawrence? Old man Valto, he was playing violin.

Is it Freddie Washington piano player? Yeah, Freddie Washington on piano. Who else was on triumphant? I can't say, I'm scared to say. You have to ask Pete, you see. Pete and Manny Manetta, see they can tell you more about it. Because I was a kid, I couldn't go down in the district. When I went down there to play, police stopped me and Lewis two, three times, you know. When they put us in jail, you know. But I told him I had a mother and didn't have no father, you see. And I had to try to help my mother make a living, you see. So he let me slide. Me and Lewis were the youngest one in there, you know. Him and I are the same age, you know. Yeah. He was born in July and I was born in September of 1900. How long have you known him, Louie? All my life. We went to school together, fifth school. I got on Padilla Street. Dated in Franklin. The principal was Arthur P. Williams. Yes, and then Lewis' kids come up together. We born in the third world, him and I both. All in the third world.
What was he like before he took out traffic? Was he playing anything else?

No, well, you see, Lewis was a kind of bad boy, you know. See, he first was out of one thing, then another. Used to sell charcoal, had charcoal schooners on the old New Basin Canal. I guess you heard about that. But he was selling charcoal out there, you know. As a kid, you know, see. Well, he wouldn't go to school. And they would pick him up and put him in jail, you know, juvenile delinquency. You know, see. The last time they put Lewis in jail, it kept him in there for indefinite legacy. Well, that's how he learned how to play the trumpet, too. Come right out the way of his home playing the trumpet. No one wasn't reading, you know. Mr. Dave tried to learn the music, but he, you know, he couldn't.
Did he sing when he was young?

No, at that time, you know, he jived around. Some of him and the boys around, they walked around for D.A. Liberty, little quartets. Him and Red Happy and Black Benny and a few more of them, you know. Just jive singing. Kids, you know, like they were doing the street jazz.
Where was Nick of Themis from here, my band?
From around there, D.A. Liberty. What did he play? No, he didn't play nothing, not as I know of.
I thought he played that, uh...

Organ? Organ. Oh, the, the, the, what the, hoody good? Yeah. Well, well, I mean, he done that for money. Oh, yeah. You see, they played, they pulled them around the street and got percentage. You see? Mm-hmm. Yeah, he used to pull the hoody good and the organ around. We call it, now y'all come the organ man, you know, see. Well, he was working, he wasn't playing nothing, you know, see. Yeah, there wasn't...
No. There wasn't any special thing without you just turning the knob on there? Just turning the knob, yeah.

Did that have a special rhythm? No, like a piano, you know. I guess, I swear it must have had in it I guess. But you turn it with your hand, you see. And they just go from corner to corner, catch the spots like that, this corner's the saloon. They play three pieces for nickels, see. You'd give them a nickel and they'd play your three numbers. Well, all right, he'd go to the next corner, they'd have anybody going to music. Now he'd play one number just to draw the people, you understand, see. Then the guy come out of the bar and he'd have drunk, say, come on man, play my nickels worth of music. Well, he'd play three numbers. Then he'd go in there, he always had his beer bucket hanging on it, all his auger. And he'd go in there and get drunk. Well, he'd play for nothing. After he'd get drunk, just keep on turning, come out there and play a tune and go in there and get him some beer and come back and play again. Sometime he'd stay there two or three hours. Sometime he'd get so drunk he couldn't pull the auger. Of course, he had to pull it, he didn't have no horse pull it, he was the horse. Boy, it was kicks, I'm telling you. It really was kicks, the auger man. And little kids would just run behind him, you know how little children are. I was in the gang running behind him too. I was small, about eight, nine years old.
He was older than Nicodemus. Oh, yeah, oh, yeah.
He was a man when we were kids.

A young man, not an old man, he was a young man, you know. He was a children. What about Shots, where was he from? Third Ward. Oh, the Third Ward. Shots was born in the Third Ward too, but not where I ran.
I don't know, but he's from the Third Ward.
How long did you know him?
Shots, I knew him a pretty good while. But I really didn't know him well until he started playing music, you see. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Did you know Stink's brother Bill Johnson? No, I didn't know him.
No, I didn't know him. No, I didn't never see him. He played banjo and face.
Yeah, that's right. What was his name?
Bill Johnson. Bill Johnson. He must have been out in Los Angeles, but I was out there, wasn't he?

Yeah, I think he was out there real early. Yeah, he did. No, he went on the road, you see. With a show? They had that Creole band with Kepa, the big ol' little. Yeah, with Kepa, I see, that's from my time.
Yeah, from my time. Yeah, from my time.
And then he went up and played with Joe Oliver. Where, Chicago? In Chicago.
Never been in Chicago in my life. I've traveled all around, never been in Chicago or New York.
Did you ever know little dad, the banjo? Oh, dad, yes, indeed.

We played a few jobs together with different bands, you know, with Lewister Maine, you see. I played with dad with Lewister Maine, just sitting in for Willigan, like Willigan couldn't play. That was Lewister's drummer, Willigan. What was his name? James Willing.
James.
Yeah, all I knew was Willigan.
See, I never knew his name.
I'm getting in. I'm getting in. This one's just off.

Yeah. Oh. Off. This down. Yeah. Yeah. We're talking about, like, he was a regular drummer. With Lewister Maine. When was that? It was in the 20s. Oh, yeah. And dad was with him then? Yeah, I think dad was playing with him.
Well, but who was, who did dad play with, regular? Did you get any information on that? Oh, yeah. We got reels at the reels. Yeah. Liberty Bell, you don't remember the Liberty Bell? Liberty Bell.
Maybe that was up when you were in Los Angeles. Yeah, I think so. Liberty Bell. Yeah. He was with Demain for a while.
Tulane, with Amos. No, with Demain. Oh, with Lewis. Yeah, with Lewis. Well, that's what I remember.
He was with Raleigh and White.
I can't remember. The Nola band. The Nola band. Who was that? Who was the leader there? Oh, gosh.
I can't remember all he, all dad told me. Punchy knew him pretty well, too. Who, Punchy?
Yeah. Oh, yeah. I imagine he did. Uh-huh. The Nola band. Who was that in the Nola band? I can't remember. Me either. Not now. I don't know. I don't know who could tell you. I don't know.
Well, dad worked with Buddy Petit football, too.
Yeah. Well, that was after my time, I guess. Yeah, I'm sure. Must have been.
I guess around the time Edmund Hall was in there. Oh, I guess so.
I see Zeb was with him, you know, when I was with him. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. But, uh, we got tape after tape on dad. Yeah. Because I knew he was about to go and he needed a little comfort, you know. Yeah. And the friendship. He liked to see punch, you know. Uh-huh. All that. You mentioned a while back something about a guitar solo, how you'd come down for that?

Yeah. How the drummer would come down. He'd hit on, he'd play on the rim, crush roll on the rims. That's the way I did most of the drummers, Henry Martin, you know. Henry Zeno, most of us, that's the way we done. Play on the rim, see. Crush roll on the rims. It's something nice. Oh. With that beat off the cymbal, you see, on your bass drum. Just like you play your bass drum now, see.
And you took the cymbal out?

Yeah, take the cymbal beat off, you see. Throw it off, you see. They were both together, you know. It's genius. And it would be a sound nice. Henry Martin was the first one I seen do it. Mm-hmm. And it sounded real nice. But the guys now, they want to scarf their rims. They got pretty drums now, you know, see. And they wouldn't want to do that, because it would make all white marks on your drum. It would be because the drum was stained dark oak. Just like the children's snare drums is now in the parade. Well, that's the way the bass drums were, the snare drums too, you see. Well, that would put marks on your drum, you know, see.
Well, when did the guitar solos start? Did they always have that when you started? I imagine they were. They were playing them way back with the Columbia band? Way back with the guitar. Yeah.
The solo stuff.
Yeah, a few of them, like solos.

Now, another fine guitar player was playing with the Silver Leaf band. What was his name? What was his name? No, no. Philip Nixon? Philip Nixon. He was a fine guitar player. Couldn't read though, you know. But, yeah. Yeah, probably a nice guitar player. Yeah, probably a nice guitar player. Did they use an ordinary flat pick or would they ever pick with their fingers or whatever? Well, I never did look at them that close. You never did notice, huh? I didn't notice that close. They said they used to play with their fingers? Some of them could, you know.
I think the sales father could, you know.
Play with his fingers.
And make all that stuff, you know. They have two runs going at once that way. Well, you don't know that.
See, I didn't pay no attention.
Those are solos.
Were they playing runs or would they play straight chords, you mean? Would they play chords about the guitar solos in the old thing you were talking about?

No, well they didn't play the solos like these boys play, just chords I imagine. Oh yeah, just straight chords. Straight chords, yeah. Up and down, yeah. Straight chords, you know. That'd be pretty loud I guess.
Oh yeah, I guess so. It was loud.
You could hear them, you know. Yeah, you could hear them. But I imagine when we was hitting that, going out of that crash, I imagine you couldn't. I imagine you couldn't.
It was too soft.
But otherwise, when you're just playing ordinary, you could hear them. Yeah.

Back before you went to California, when you were very young, how would the bands play a piece? How you mean? Well, I mean, would they start off loud or soft? Would everybody come in on the beginning?

Yeah, everybody. Everybody. It's like you're shocking them, everybody playing. Ensemble. That's right. That's right. That's right. That would be the beginning, huh? In the beginning. Then all right, if you had your trumpet player, he wanted to take a solo, well you let him take a solo. You take two, you're a trombone player, you're a clarinet player. But most was ensemble, see. Didn't do very much soloing, see. Didn't do very much. All the bands, just like you hear Shark and Al Wakeman play, well that's the way they was playing.
But more ensemble. Yeah, oh yeah, yeah.

All together, you know, all the Dixie Langues, we call it Dixie Langues, we call it break time then, you know, see. But it's the same, mean the same thing. We call it J-A-S-S first, then it comes to J-A-Z-Z. Doesn't mean all the same, yeah, see.
Well, at that time, you say you'd have your ensemble first. About how many choruses ensemble?

Oh, they'd play about three. About three on the choruses. Yeah, all together. Yeah, you see they play all. Now my idea, when they first started to play them solos, when they got the banjos? Yeah, the banjos. Yeah, you see. That guy was playing with us, Buddy Malady, you see, was playing with Buddy. When I was playing with Buddy, the guy was playing with Sam. Caffrey was playing on the roof guard. Now he was a fine solo man, little Caffrey. Fine. He couldn't read it, but I wish he had to get the banjo he would play.
And that was after you came back.
Yeah, see that was after I came back. So before they didn't have too much solo. No, didn't have too much. No, they didn't have too much before I left.
Well, say you had at that early period, before California, say you finished that three choruses ensemble, who would take down?

Who would take down? Yeah. Well, if the trumpet player might want to take a solo. Oh, after three ensembles he'd still be strong enough? Man, Celestine looked like he played for hours. Man, Celestine was playing up on the bandstand with us at the temple, I swear to God. He played a tune so long it was pitiful. I'm telling you, it was not nastush, you know. Ain't nothing but chorus. It's the same thing, you know. Man, that man would play chorus, man, after chorus, chorus after chorus. Wouldn't allow us to play nothing. Man, he went over there and asked him, say, what you doing, man, playing about a hour or what? That answer he played so long, I thought, oh, man. He'd take down and the trombone and all the rest of them would play. All right, he'd put up. Then the trombone, I guess he's tired, that's why he'd take now, you know. And the clarinet, then he'd put up, the trombone put up. Then him and Celestine would play. Then the clarinet would take down. Nothing but the rhythm, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump.
Then they'd pick up a, oh, man, I swear to God, that people played so long, man. Oh, man.

Now, the only time they would play short, they'd play orchestration, you see. Well, they'd play it down. And if it was a good orchestration, you know, that they liked, well, they'd go back to the chorus and play one or two, you see. Of course, Celestine always read music, just like Manuel Perez, you see. Always had musicians in their reach, you know. It felt like Buddy Pettine, you know.

You know, when I used to go out to Tyler's Beer Garden? Who? To Tyler's Beer Garden during the war. I don't think you were ever out there. No, I don't. But Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman had the band. Tillman played with us?
Yeah.
Tillman was playing saxophone. Tillman was playing saxophone.
What year that was?

Forty-five. Oh, no. I wasn't there. And Dude was playing trumpet with him, Foster and Brother. And Dude would take down, but the clarinet would, I mean the saxophone would carry the melody and the trombone would still play tailgate. And then Dude would come back. Who was on trombone?
Joe Avery. Oh, Joe Avery.
But I never heard a solo the whole time I was there, you know.
They didn't play a solo.
I wondered how many bands there were like that that would, uh.
Just play like that.
Where the trumpet would take down and that would be the only guy that would ever take
down.

What? Yeah, that's right. Did they ever have bands like that when you remember? I might have been. I don't know. I just wondered if they had any guys that played clarinet and trombone together, you know, would really be featured like that.

Be featured like? Like solos, trombone and clarinet? Well a duet really, the two of the together. Oh no, hardly. Hardly, huh? Hardly. Because you know they didn't know that much about music to play on. Cards you know. They just played on. Well I don't mean cards. I mean tailgate. Yeah. But I know like Yank and them used to play. But most of the time when Buddy would take a solo in our band, they would take down, you see. Now when I was playing with Ridley, when David Jones would take a solo, the bands would take down. And I used to get after them about that because you know, see, everybody would take down, you see. It looked like the bottom would fall out, you see. Nothing but jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, and one man up there playing, you see. Nothing but jump. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

segments.title: Recording setup and opening question about society jobs
segments.summary: Interviewers note the recording location and date and start asking about the jobs he played.

segments.title: Seasonal society jobs: debutantes, Boston Club, Monteleone
segments.summary: Williams describes the yearly round of Christmas, debutante, Mardi Gras and country club jobs played by a ten-piece band, and the move to the Monteleone ballroom.

segments.title: Whether Sam Morgan and Buddy Petit played parades
segments.summary: Williams says they were hired for parades but not funerals because they could not read well enough.

segments.title: Brass bands and funeral hymns
segments.summary: Names other brass bands and explains that non-readers played funerals by ear; he recalls the first hymns bands played coming back.

segments.title: Playing at Pete Lala's with Joe Oliver's band, and growing up with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He took over Oliver's job at Pete Lala's with a small band including Armstrong, and recalls police stopping the young players and that he and Louis were born in 1900 and went to school together.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong as a boy: charcoal, jail and learning trumpet
segments.summary: Williams describes Louis as a bad boy who sold charcoal, was jailed, and learned trumpet there.

segments.title: Street quartet singing with Red Happy and Black Benny
segments.summary: As kids Louis and others sang jive quartets in the street.

segments.title: The organ man pulling his hurdy-gurdy through the streets
segments.summary: Williams describes the street organ man who played three tunes for a nickel and drank beer, with kids running behind.

segments.title: Where Shots was from, and Bill Johnson on banjo
segments.summary: Brief exchanges about Shots's origins and Bill Johnson, who went on tour with the Creole band; Williams was never in Chicago or New York.

segments.title: Little Dad the banjoist and the bands he played with
segments.summary: Williams sat in for drummer Willigan in Louis Dumaine's band with Little Dad; they try to recall Dad's other bands, including the Nola band and Buddy Petit.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Drum breaks: playing the rims for guitar solos
segments.summary: He explains how drummers like Henry Martin played crush rolls on the rims and why modern drummers avoid it.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Guitar playing in the old bands, Philip Nixon and straight chords
segments.summary: Discussion of early guitar solos; Williams recalls Philip Nixon and says guitarists played straight chords.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Ensemble playing, the word jazz, and the arrival of banjo solos
segments.summary: Early bands played mostly ensemble, about three choruses, with few solos until banjoists like Caffrey came after he returned.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Celestin playing endless choruses at the Temple
segments.summary: He tells of Celestin soloing chorus after chorus while others took down, and that orchestrations were played short.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Tyler's Beer Garden band with Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman
segments.summary: The interviewer describes a 1945 band with saxophone, trumpet and tailgate trombone that never soloed.

segments.chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
segments.title: Whether bands featured trombone and clarinet; everyone laying out for a solo
segments.summary: Williams says duets were rare and recalls everyone dropping out behind a soloist in Buddy's and Ridgley's bands.
